terms.grammar: phrase: fallō, fallere, fefellī, falsum, with spem (or opīniōnem, expectation) and the genitive or possessive of the person
evidence: Cic. Fam. 1.6.2: nōn fallam opīniōnem tuam
Cic. Fam. 1.9.16: in quō ego spem fefellī … invidōrum
terms.comment: Latin says what is disappointed: the hope (spem) or the expectation (opīniōnem, exspectātiōnem). The hope can be the subject too: nē spēs eum fallat, so that he is not disappointed (Cic. Fam. 1.3, Lewis & Short). Alone, fallere is to deceive.

evidence: Ter. And. 374: saepe jam mē spēs haec frūstrāta est
terms.comment: From frūstrā, in vain: to make someone’s hope or effort come to nothing; also to deceive, to trick (Lewis & Short). In a passive sense, frūstrātus spē, disappointed in a hope (Vell. 2.21.2, Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: phrase: the passive of dējiciō with the ablative spē
evidence: Caes. BG 1.8.4 (Lewis & Short): eā spē dējectī
terms.comment: Literally “thrown down from a hope”: the historians’ way of saying that a hope came to nothing.

phrases.latin: Ā mē omnia summa in tē studia officiaque exspectā; nōn fallam opīniōnem tuam.
phrases.english: Expect every devotion and service from me; I won’t disappoint you.

phrases.latin: Ībō: etsī hercle saepe jam mē spēs haec frūstrāta est.
phrases.english: I’ll go, though heaven knows this hope has often let me down before.

phrases.latin: Vah, frūstrā sum igitur gāvīsus miser.
phrases.english: Oh, so I was glad for nothing, poor me.

phrases.latin: nōlī affectāre quod tibi nōn est datum, dēlūsa nē spēs ad querēlam reccidat
phrases.english: don’t reach for what wasn’t given you, or your disappointed hope will fall back into complaint

long-u.html: Made from frūstrā (Lewis & Short), whose u is long: de Vaan s.v. fraus derives it from *fraud-tro-, and Bennett cites an apex.

sources: Lewis & Short: fallo · Lewis & Short: frustror · Lewis & Short: deicio · Lewis & Short: spes
